quotes.whole:
A user agent MUST dispatch this event when a mouse wheel has
been rotated around any axis, or when an equivalent input device
(such as a mouse-ball, certain tablets or touchpads, etc.) has
emulated such an action. Depending on the platform and input device,
diagonal wheel deltas MAY be delivered either as a single wheel event with multiple non-zero axes or as separate wheel events for each non-zero axis.
The typical default action of the wheel event type is
to scroll (or in some cases, zoom) the document by the indicated
amount.  If this event is canceled, the implementation MUST NOT
scroll or zoom the document (or perform whatever other
implementation-specific default action is associated with this event
type).
In some user agents, or with some input devices, the speed
that the wheel has been turned can affect the delta values,
with a faster speed producing a higher delta value.

quotes.whole:
Numerous clarifications to the interfaces and event types have been made.
The HTMLEvents module is no longer defined in this document.
The focus and blur events have been added to the UIEvent module, and the dblclick event has been added to the MouseEvent module. This new specification provides a better separation between the DOM
event flow, the event types, and the DOM interfaces.
12.1.1. Changes to DOM Level 2 event flow
This new specification introduced the following new concepts in the
event flow:
Event listeners are now ordered. In DOM Level 2, the event ordering
was unspecified.
The event flow now includes the Window, to
reflect existing implementations.
12.1.2. Changes to DOM Level 2 event types
Many clarifications have been made on the event types. The conformance
is now explicitly defined against the event types, and not only in terms
of interfaces used by the event types.
"MutationEvents" have been deprecated. Support for
namespaced events, present in early drafts of this specification, has
also been removed.
For user agents which support the DOMNodeInserted and DOMNodeRemoved event types, this specification no longer requires
that the event type be fired for Attr nodes.

quotes.whole:
Numerous clarifications to the interfaces and event types have been made.
The HTMLEvents module is no longer defined in this document.
The focus and blur events have been added to the UIEvent module, and the dblclick event has been added to the MouseEvent module. This new specification provides a better separation between the DOM
event flow, the event types, and the DOM interfaces.
12.1.1. Changes to DOM Level 2 event flow
This new specification introduced the following new concepts in the
event flow:
Event listeners are now ordered. In DOM Level 2, the event ordering
was unspecified.
The event flow now includes the Window, to
reflect existing implementations.

Many clarifications have been made on the event types. The conformance
is now explicitly defined against the event types, and not only in terms
of interfaces used by the event types.
"MutationEvents" have been deprecated. Support for
namespaced events, present in early drafts of this specification, has
also been removed.
For user agents which support the DOMNodeInserted and DOMNodeRemoved event types, this specification no longer requires
that the event type be fired for Attr nodes.

quotes.whole:
UI Events
UI Events
Concepts and Usage
The UI Events API defines a system for handling user interactions such as mouse and keyboard input. This includes:
events that are fired on specific user actions such key presses or mouse clicks. Most of these events fire on the Element interface, but the events relating to loading and unloading resources fire on the Window interface.
event interfaces, which are passed into handlers for these events. These interfaces inherit from Event and provide extra information specific to the type of user interaction: for example, the KeyboardEvent is passed into a keydown event handler and provides information about the key that was pressed.
In this article
Concepts and Usage
Interfaces
Events
Examples
Specifications
See also
Interfaces
CompositionEvent
Passed into handlers for composition events. Composition events enable a user to enter characters that might not be available on the physical keyboard.
FocusEvent
Passed into handlers for focus events, which are associated with elements receiving or losing focus.
InputEvent
Passed into handlers for input events, which are associated with the user entering some input; for example, using an <input> element.

verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE MEMO — UI Events, wheel event type

1. BOTTOM LINE (ask 1)

The event type a user agent is required to dispatch when a mouse wheel is rotated is **`wheel`** (interface `WheelEvent`). It is a single lowercase token: `wheel`. Legacy types `mousewheel` and `DOMMouseScroll` are NOT defined by UI Events and are not acceptable substitutes for conformance.

2. WHAT THE SPECIFICATION SAYS ABOUT THAT SECTION (ask 2)

2.1 Revision control — read this first, because the answer's *location* moved.

The wheel event type is defined in the UI Events drafts of 2022–2024. In the **current** UI Events draft at https://www.w3.org/TR/uievents/ the section is gone; it says, verbatim:

  “The Mouse Events and Wheel Events section of this specification have been moved to the Pointer Events specification [pointerevents4].”

So: same answer (`wheel`), different home. A reviewer auditing against the newest draft must read Pointer Events Level 4 for the normative wheel definition; a reviewer auditing against the 2022–2024 WDs will find it in UI Events. State which revision you audited, and cite it.

Section numbering by revision (from the documents' own headers in the retrieved text):
- W3C UI Events WD 29 June 2022 — §5.4.2.1 `wheel`, §5.4.2.2 cancelability of wheel events.
- W3C UI Events WD 21 February 2024 — §5.4.2.1 `wheel`, §5.4.2.2 cancelability of wheel events.
- W3C UI Events WD 13 June 2024 — §4.5.2.1 `wheel`, §4.5.2.2 cancelability of wheel events.
- W3C UI Events WD 13 June 2026 — NOT VERIFIED. The retrieved excerpt from that draft contained no wheel passage, so no section number is asserted here. Confirm at source before citing.
- W3C UI Events living draft (/TR/uievents/) — section removed, see the pointerevents4 note above.

2.2 The normative requirement, verbatim (identical text in all three verified revisions):

  “A user agent MUST dispatch this event when a mouse wheel has been rotated around any axis, or when an equivalent input device (such as a mouse-ball, certain tablets or touchpads, etc.) has emulated such an action. Depending on the platform and input device, diagonal wheel deltas MAY be delivered either as a single wheel event with multiple non-zero axes or as separate wheel events for each non-zero axis.

  The typical default action of the wheel event type is to scroll (or in some cases, zoom) the document by the indicated amount. If this event is canceled, the implementation MUST NOT scroll or zoom the document (or perform whatever other implementation-specific default action is associated with this event type).

  In some user agents, or with some input devices, the speed that the wheel has been turned can affect the delta values, with a faster speed producing a higher delta value.”

2.3 Section summary — what is normative vs. informative, statement by statement:

| Statement | Level | Compliance consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Dispatch on wheel rotation about ANY axis, or on an equivalent emulating device | MUST | Mandatory. Note “any axis”: vertical-only implementations are non-conforming. Equivalent devices (trackballs, some tablets/touchpads) are in scope. |
| Diagonal deltas as one multi-axis event OR as separate per-axis events | MAY | Implementation choice; either is conforming. Do not fail an implementation for picking one. |
| Default action is to scroll (sometimes zoom) the document by the indicated amount | Descriptive (“typical”) | Characterises expected behaviour; not itself a MUST. |
| If canceled, MUST NOT scroll/zoom or run the implementation-specific default action | MUST NOT | Mandatory once the event is canceled. This is the testable teeth of the section. |
| Wheel speed can affect delta magnitude | Informative | No conformance requirement; explains why delta magnitudes are not normalised. |

2.4 The cancelability subsection (§4.5.2.2 / §5.4.2.2), quoted to the point of truncation in the source excerpt:

  “Calling preventDefault on a wheel event can prevent or otherwise interrupt scrolling. For maximum scroll performance, a user agent may not wait for each wheel event associated with the scroll to be processed to see if it will be canceled. In such cases the user…”

  [The retrieved excerpt is truncated mid-sentence. Do NOT complete that sentence from memory in a compliance filing — re-fetch the section and quote it in full.] The operative compliance point that IS fully captured: `preventDefault()` on a wheel event is expected to suppress scrolling, and the spec explicitly acknowledges that a user agent may process scrolling before cancellation is known (the basis for passive-listener semantics in browsers).

2.5 Section metadata table (Type / Interface / Bubbles / Cancelable / Composed / Trusted Targets / Default action).

  [recall — verify] The section's summary table is not present in the retrieved excerpt. Per the UI Events wheel definition the rows are expected to be: Type `wheel`; Interface `WheelEvent`; Sync/Async Async; Bubbles Yes; Trusted Targets `Window`, `Document`, `Element`; Cancelable Yes; Composed Yes; Default action scroll/zoom. Cite these from the source page, not from this memo, in any filing.

2.6 Related / legacy events.

UI Events defines only `wheel` for this input. Corroborated in the retrieved MDN text: “MouseScrollEvent — Deprecated, Firefox-only, non-standard interface for scroll events. Use WheelEvent instead.” `mousewheel` (WebKit/IE heritage) and `DOMMouseScroll` (Firefox heritage) are non-standard; their presence in a codebase is a portability finding, not a UI Events conformance finding.

3. RESOLVING “DOCUMENT WHEEL”

UI Events defines no term “document wheel”. Two readings, both answered:
- If it means “the user rotates a wheel while the document is the interaction context”: the required type is `wheel`, and its trusted targets include `Document` and `Window`, so a document-level listener is a legitimate observation point.
- If it means “the wheel's default action scrolls the document”: that is the described typical default action, and it MUST NOT occur if the event is canceled.

In both readings the dispatched type is `wheel`. The event is dispatched at the element under the pointer and propagates through Document and Window.

4. HOW TO VERIFY CONFORMANCE (procedure for the reviewer)

Step 1 — pin the revision. Record the exact URL and date of the UI Events draft audited (e.g. https://www.w3.org/TR/2024/WD-uievents-20240613/), or, if auditing the living draft, note that the wheel definition now lives in Pointer Events L4 and cite that instead.

Step 2 — probe the implementation in a real browser with a real (trusted) wheel. Script-synthesised wheel events cannot prove conformance because `isTrusted` will be false and the default action will not run.

```js
// Paste in the page under review; then physically scroll the wheel over the page.
const seen = [];
document.addEventListener('wheel', (e) => {
  seen.push({
    type: e.type,              // expect 'wheel'
    ctor: e.constructor.name,  // expect 'WheelEvent'
    isTrusted: e.isTrusted,    // must be true for a user-generated wheel
    target: e.target.nodeName || String(e.target),
    bubbles: e.bubbles,        // expect true
    cancelable: e.cancelable,  // expect true
    composed: e.composed,      // expect true
    deltaMode: e.deltaMode,    // 0=pixel, 1=line, 2=page  [recall — verify against IDL]
    deltaX: e.deltaX, deltaY: e.deltaY, deltaZ: e.deltaZ
  });
}, { capture: true, passive: true });
console.table(seen);
```

Step 3 — default-action suppression test. Attach a non-passive listener that calls `preventDefault()`, scroll with the wheel, and confirm the viewport does not move (MUST NOT scroll). Then remove it and confirm scrolling resumes. If the listener is registered as passive, cancellation is ignored by design — do not record that as a spec violation; record it as a listener-configuration observation.

Step 4 — diagonal test. Scroll diagonally (or use a trackpad two-finger diagonal gesture). Either a single `wheel` event with both `deltaX` and `deltaY` non-zero, or two `wheel` events each with one non-zero axis, is conforming (MAY).

Step 5 — legacy audit. Grep the codebase for `mousewheel` and `DOMMouseScroll`. Findings here are non-standard-API findings; the fix is to listen for `wheel` only.

5. PASS/FAIL CRITERIA FOR THE REVIEW

PASS: a trusted `wheel` event is observed on wheel rotation; `type === 'wheel'`; `preventDefault()` on a non-passive listener suppresses the scroll/zoom default action; diagonal deltas arrive as one multi-axis event or as separate per-axis events.

FAIL: no `wheel` dispatched; `wheel` not cancelable; scroll still occurs after a successful `preventDefault()` on a non-passive listener; vertical-only dispatch on a device capable of horizontal input (violates “around any axis”).

NOT A FAILURE: choice of one-vs-many diagonal events; large or speed-dependent delta magnitudes; passive-listener cancellation being ignored.

6. ITEMS TO CONFIRM AT SOURCE BEFORE FILING

(a) The exact section number in the 2026-06-13 WD — not captured. (b) The full text of the cancelability paragraph beyond the truncation. (c) The section's metadata table rows. (d) Whether the living draft's pointerevents4 pointer resolves to Pointer Events Level 4 and what that document's wheel definition says — it supersedes this memo's location, not its answer.

verdict.summary:
NERC PRC-024-3 COMPLIANCE ANSWER — SETTING-PROVISION TIMEFRAME, POST-CHANGE DEADLINE AND EXCEPTION, AND R1–R4 EVIDENCE RETENTION

1. SCOPE, SOURCES AND VERSION PREMISE

Ask 1 is a scoping constraint, not a question with a value: every figure below is read from the standard text of NERC PRC-024-3, 'Frequency and Voltage Protection Settings for Generating Resources', fetched from https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/standards/reliability-standards/prc/prc-024-3.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23T21:25:58Z, sha256 941a2187c37f).

Version/date caveat (stated, not papered over): the fetched documents establish that the NERC Board of Trustees adopted PRC-024-3 on February 6, 2020, that the filing proposed a 24-month implementation period, and that Canadian filings (New Brunswick, Alberta) and a Quebec form exist for PRC-024-3 — but no fetched page states the regulatory effective date in any jurisdiction. The premise 'as in force on 2026-11-21' is therefore accepted as supplied by the requester. The answers below do not depend on a different revision's wording: the same two figures (60 calendar days; 3 years or until the next audit, whichever is longer) also appear in the PRC-024-2 text that the AESO file actually contains, so the numbers are stable across the two revisions even though the R4 phrasing differs (PRC-024-2: 'generator protection trip settings ... associated unit'; PRC-024-3: 'applicable protection settings ... generating resource(s)').

Document hygiene note: https://www.aeso.ca/assets/Uploads/PRC-024-3.pdf (sha256 58fabb8ef6ed) is named for PRC-024-3 but its body is headed 'Standard PRC-024-2 — Generator Frequency and Voltage Protective Relay Settings'. It is usable only as corroboration of the 60-day and 3-year figures; its R4 wording must not be quoted as PRC-024-3.

2. ASK 2 — TIME TO PROVIDE R1/R2 PROTECTION SETTINGS AFTER A WRITTEN REQUEST: 60 CALENDAR DAYS

PRC-024-3, Requirement R4 (verbatim, NERC PRC-024-3 page): 'Each Generator Owner shall provide its applicable protection settings associated with Requirements R1 and R2 to the Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner that models the associated generating resource(s) within 60 calendar days of receipt of a written request for the data and within 60 calendar days of any change to those previously requested settings unless directed by the requesting Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner that the reporting of protection setting changes is not required.' [Violation Risk Factor: Lower] [Time Horizon: Operations Planning]

Answer: 60 calendar days, measured from RECEIPT of the written request (not from the date the request was written or mailed), and only where the request comes from the Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner that models the associated generating resource(s). A request from any other entity does not start this clock under R4.

Associated evidence obligation, M4 (verbatim): 'Each Generator Owner shall have evidence that it communicated applicable protection settings in accordance with Requirement R4, such as dated e-mails, correspondence or other evidence and copies of any requests it has received for that information.'

3. ASK 3 — POST-CHANGE DEADLINE AND EXCEPTION

Deadline after a change: the same 60 calendar days, running from the change to the previously requested settings ('within 60 calendar days of any change to those previously requested settings'). The clock starts at the change itself, not at any later notice of it.

Exception (the identifier reported for ask 3): 'unless directed by the requesting Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner that the reporting of protection setting changes is not required.' Operationally: if the PC/TP that models the resource has directed that changes need not be reported, the post-change 60-day reporting obligation is excused; absent such a direction, the 60-day clock runs. The direction is itself a document to be obtained and kept — M4 requires evidence of communication and copies of requests, and a direction that reporting is not required is the evidence that explains a missing post-change submittal.

4. ASK 4 — RETENTION FOR REQUIREMENTS R1 THROUGH R4: 3 YEARS, OR UNTIL THE NEXT AUDIT, WHICHEVER IS LONGER

PRC-024-3, Section 1.2 Data Retention (verbatim, NERC PRC-024-3 page): 'The Generator Owner shall keep data or evidence Requirement R1 through R4; for 3 years or until the next audit, whichever is longer.'

Answer: 3 years — but 3 years is a FLOOR, not a cap. The operative retention period is the later of (a) three years from creation of the evidence and (b) the conclusion of the next audit covering the period. If the next audit falls four years out, the evidence must be kept four years.

Note on the proofs of absence: the harness searched the full text of the NB filing (https://www.nerc.com/FilingsOrders/ca/Canadian%20Filings%20and%20Orders%20DL/NB%20PRC-024-3%20Filing.pdf, sha256 715329814103), the Alberta filing (https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/who-we-are/legal--regulatory/ca/filings--orders/alberta-prc-024-3-filing.pdf, sha256 c1925f40cea0) and the Quebec QRS form (https://www.regie-energie.qc.ca/.../qrsaw-prc-024-3-v1en.docx, sha256 c86d14b93647) for 'three (3) years', '3 years', 'three years', 'retention', 'retain' and 'data or evidence' and found none of them. Those pages are petitions and a compliance form and are silent on retention; the answer is therefore not 'the page states none'. The figure is taken from the standard text page, which states it expressly, so ask 4 is answered, not listed as not stated.

Adjacent clause worth noting for the retention procedure (quoted from the PRC-024-2 text in the AESO file, not visible in the PRC-024-3 excerpt fetched): an entity found non-compliant keeps information related to the non-compliance until mitigation is complete and approved, for the longer of that period and the period above. Treat this as a conservative practice rule until the PRC-024-3 Data Retention section is read in full.

5. DISTINCTIONS THAT PREVENT MISREADING THE FIGURES

- 150 calendar days is NOT the requirement. It appears only in the Violation Severity Level tables as the Severe VSL threshold ('failed to provide protection settings within 150 calendar days of a written request', '...within 150 calendar days of any change'). It describes how bad a violation is, not an allowed timeframe. The compliant deadline remains 60 calendar days; the VSL bands (more than 60 up to 90, more than 90 up to 120, more than 120 up to 150, and beyond 150) all sit above the 60-day requirement, which confirms 60 is the limit.
- 30 calendar days is NOT the answer. It is Requirement R3.1, the separate obligation to communicate a documented regulatory or equipment limitation (or the removal of one) to the Planning Coordinator and Transmission Planner.
- The Quebec Interconnection variance (Section D.A.) does not change the 60-day figure. It extends R4 to 'Generator Owner and Transmission Owner' and points R4 at Requirements R1 and D.A.2 rather than R1 and R2, but the timeframe wording is identical: 'within 60 calendar days of receipt of a written request for the data and within 60 calendar days of any change to those previously requested settings unless directed by the requesting Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner that the reporting of protection setting changes is not required.' Other regional or jurisdictional supplements are entity-specific and are not addressed by the fetched pages.

6. IMPLEMENTATION PROCEDURE FOR A GENERATOR OWNER

Step 1 — Intake and qualification. On receipt of any request for R1/R2 protection settings, log: date received, requesting entity, and a determination that the requester is the Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner that models the resource. If it is not, R4's clock is not triggered by that request (other obligations may still apply).
Step 2 — Start the clock at receipt. Example: written request received 2026-11-21 → R4 response due 2027-01-20 (60 calendar days).
Step 3 — Deliver and evidence. Send the applicable R1 and R2 protection settings (setting sheets, voltage-time boundaries, calibration sheets, coordination plots, dynamic simulation studies, calculations) and retain the dated transmittal (email or letter) plus a copy of the request, per M4.
Step 4 — Change control. Any change to previously requested settings triggers a fresh 60-calendar-day clock from the date of the change. Example: setting changed 2027-03-01 → report due 2027-04-30. Log the change date at the moment the setting is changed, not when someone remembers to report it.
Step 5 — Exception handling. If the requesting PC/TP directs that reporting of protection setting changes is not required, record the direction (dated email or letter) in the R4 file and do not report that change; without a written direction, report it.
Step 6 — Retention. Keep all R1–R4 data and evidence for at least 3 years or until the next audit, whichever is longer; keep non-compliance records until mitigation is complete and approved. Practically: set the retention date to the later of (evidence date + 3 years) and (conclusion of the next audit covering the period), and do not purge on a fixed 3-year cycle.

7. CONSOLIDATED ANSWERS

Ask 2: 60 calendar days from receipt of the written request from the PC/TP that models the resource(s).
Ask 3: 60 calendar days from the change, with the exception that the change need not be reported if the requesting PC/TP directs that reporting of protection setting changes is not required.
Ask 4: 3 years, or until the next audit, whichever is longer (3 years is the floor).

quotes.whole:
Editorial Note on Part 1926




Editorial Notes:


Nomenclature changes to part 1926 appear at 84 FR 21597, May 14, 2019.






§ 1926.441 Batteries and battery charging.




(a) General requirements. 




(1) Batteries of the unsealed type shall be located in enclosures with outside vents or in well ventilated rooms and shall be arranged so as to prevent the escape of fumes, gases, or electrolyte spray into other areas.






(2) Ventilation shall be provided to ensure diffusion of the gases from the battery and to prevent the accumulation of an explosive mixture.






(3) Racks and trays shall be substantial and shall be treated to make them resistant to the electrolyte.






(4) Floors shall be of acid resistant construction unless protected from acid accumulations.






(5) Face shields, aprons, and rubber gloves shall be provided for workers handling acids or batteries.






(6) Facilities for quick drenching of the eyes and body shall be provided within 25 feet (7.62 m) of battery handling areas.






(7) Facilities shall be provided for flushing and neutralizing spilled electrolyte and for fire protection.








(b) Charging. 




(1) Battery charging installations shall be located in areas designated for that purpose.






(2) Charging apparatus shall be protected from damage by trucks.





(3) When batteries are being charged, the vent caps shall be kept in place to avoid electrolyte spray. Vent caps shall be maintained in functioning condition.

ANSWER

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart K (Electrical), as in force on 2026-11-21, facilities for quick drenching of the eyes and body must be provided within 25 feet (7.62 m) of battery handling areas.

GOVERNING PROVISION

29 CFR 1926.441(a)(6) — Batteries and battery charging, General requirements:

  "Facilities for quick drenching of the eyes and body shall be provided within 25 feet (7.62 m) of battery handling areas."

Location within the part: 29 CFR part 1926, subpart K (Electrical), § 1926.441 "Batteries and battery charging," paragraph (a) "General requirements," item (6). Section 1926.441 sits under the subpart's division "Safety Requirements for Special Equipment" (§§ 1926.433–1926.440 reserved; § 1926.441; §§ 1926.442–1926.448 reserved; § 1926.449 definitions). The subpart's stated scope (§ 1926.400) is "electrical safety requirements that are necessary for the practical safeguarding of employees involved in construction work."

NUMERIC VALUE AND UNIT CONVERSION

  25 feet = 7.62 m (25 × 0.3048 = 7.62 exactly), the conversion the regulation itself prints in parentheses.

The requirement is a maximum permissible distance: the drenching facility must be no farther than 25 ft from the battery handling area. It is not a minimum setback.

CURRENCY AS OF 2026-11-21

Text verified against two independent official renderings that both reproduce § 1926.441(a)(6) with the identical "within 25 feet (7.62 m)" wording:
  - eCFR, 29 CFR 1926.441 (current): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/part-1926/section-1926.441
  - eCFR, 29 CFR part 1926 subpart K landing page: https://ecfr.gov/current/title-29/part-1926/subpart-K
  - U.S. Government Publishing Office, CFR 2025 print edition, title 29, vol. 8, § 1926.441 (and § 1926.449, same volume): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title29-vol8/pdf/CFR-2025-title29-vol8-sec1926-449.pdf
  - OSHA standard page: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1926/1926.441

Honest limit on date verification: the retrievals were made 2026-11-23, two days after the target date of 2026-11-21, and "current" eCFR reflects the point of retrieval, not an arbitrary historical date. The 2025 annual print edition (which is fixed and cannot change) and the current eCFR agree word-for-word, so the provision's wording is stable across the interval spanning 2026-11-21. If a user requires point-in-time certification for that exact date, the definitive check is the eCFR point-in-time view (ecfr.gov "View as of" 2026-11-21) or the Federal Register documents affecting part 1926 in the 2025–2026 window; nothing in the retrieved material indicates any amendment to § 1926.441.

WHAT COUNTS AS A "BATTERY HANDLING AREA"

Section 1926.441 does not define the term, but the paragraph structure supplies its scope: it covers areas where batteries or electrolyte are handled — battery changing/removal and replacement, watering, terminal connection/disconnection, and the designated charging installations required by § 1926.441(b)(1) ("Battery charging installations shall be located in areas designated for that purpose"). Practical consequence: the 25 ft envelope must be measured from the boundary of every such area, not merely from a single central charging bench, and it must be satisfied for each area where the exposure exists.

MEASUREMENT AND SITING NOTES FOR FIELD APPLICATION

  - Distance is measured as the actual route an exposed employee must travel from the battery handling area to the drenching facility, not straight-line through walls, racks, or equipment. A facility 20 ft away as the crow flies but behind a locked door 60 ft down a corridor does not satisfy "within 25 feet."
  - The path must be unobstructed and immediately available during battery handling; a unit blocked by a parked forklift or stored pallets fails the requirement regardless of tape-measure distance.
  - The 25 ft limit is a ceiling, not a target. Closer placement is compliant and is the safer design choice given that eye/skin contact with sulfuric acid electrolyte is the hazard addressed by § 1926.441(a)(5)–(7).
  - The same paragraph independently requires, at § 1926.441(a)(7), "facilities ... for flushing and neutralizing spilled electrolyte and for fire protection" — a separate obligation that the drenching facility alone does not discharge.
  - Nothing in § 1926.441(a)(6) prescribes a flow rate, water temperature, tepid-water control, or weekly activation test. Those are general-industry emergency-shower performance expectations (ANSI/ISEA Z358.1, incorporated by reference in OSHA's 1910.151(c) compliance guidance), not requirements written into 1926 Subpart K. Specifying a Z358.1-compliant unit is a reasonable means of satisfying "facilities for quick drenching," but the enforceable distance limit for construction work remains the 25 ft in § 1926.441(a)(6).

SCOPE BOUNDARY — CONSTRUCTION VS. GENERAL INDUSTRY (do not conflate)

  - Construction (29 CFR 1926, subpart K): numeric limit — within 25 ft (7.62 m). This governs the question as asked.
  - General industry (29 CFR 1910.151(c)): no numeric distance; it requires suitable facilities for quick drenching "within the work area for quick drenching of the eyes and body." Qualitative, and it does not supply a 25 ft figure.
  - Because the ask is expressly limited to 1926 Subpart K, 25 ft is the answer. 1910.151(c) is cited here only to prevent the two standards from being mixed.

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE RECORD

Maximum permitted distance from a battery handling area to the quick-drenching facility for eyes and body, under 29 CFR 1926.441(a)(6) as in force 2026-11-21: 25 feet (7.62 m).

A user agent MUST dispatch this event when a text composition system is enabled and a new composition session is about to begin (or has begun, depending on the text composition system) in preparation for composing a passage of text. This event type is device-dependent, and MAY rely upon the capabilities of the text conversion system and how it is mapped into the operating system. When a keyboard is used to feed an input method editor, this event type is generated after a keydown event, but speech or handwriting recognition systems MAY send this event type without keyboard events. Some implementations MAY populate the data attribute of the compositionstart event with the text currently selected in the document (for editing and replacement). Otherwise, the value of the data attribute MUST be the empty string.
This event MUST be dispatched immediately before a text composition system begins a new composition session, and before the DOM is modified due to the composition process. The default action of this event is for the text composition system to start a new composition session. If this event is canceled, the text composition system SHOULD discard the current composition session.
Canceling the compositionstart event type is distinct from canceling the text composition system itself (e.g., by hitting a cancel button or closing an IME window). Some IMEs do not support cancelling an in-progress composition session (e.g., such as GTK which doesn’t presently have such an API). In these cases, calling preventDefault() will not stop this event’s default action.

The UI Events API defines a system for handling user interactions such as mouse and keyboard input. This includes:
events that are fired on specific user actions such key presses or mouse clicks. Most of these events fire on the Element interface, but the events relating to loading and unloading resources fire on the Window interface.

DETAILS
The reported UFLS entity “Total Load (MW)” is the sum of that Entities “Total Forecasted

LOAD SHED
The initial draft version of the Inventory DB posted by SPP PC contains load shed by
frequency based on the previously submitted UFLS data for your entity, i.e. 2014. The
previous load values have been replaced with the current models values. If the load bus
number was changed from the previous model the data will NOT appear in this
spreadsheet. Also, it may be possible for new loads to have been introduced into the
current model, so take care to include those as necessary. Loads that have been removed
from the previous model have been removed from this spreadsheet.
Load shed amounts (PX) are estimates from the previously submitted UFLS data and
represent the sum of all distribution feeder loads tripped. The load shed at a specific
frequency (FR) is the new models load (PL) multiplied by the fraction of the previous data
submittal for that load.

verdict.summary:
NERC PRC-024-3 — Protection-setting submittal time limits (Requirement R4) and data/evidence retention (Requirements R1–R4), as in force on 2026-11-21

1. STANDARD VERSION APPLICABLE ON 2026-11-21
Standard: PRC-024-3, "Frequency and Voltage Protection Settings for Generating Resources" (NERC Reliability Standard).
Source of the requirement text: https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/standards/reliability-standards/prc/prc-024-3.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23T21:51:48Z, sha256 941a2187c37f) — read in full.
Effective date: October 1, 2022 (ReliabilityFirst PRC-024-3 presentation, 16 May 2022, https://www.rfirst.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/PRC-024-3-Presentation_16May2022.pdf). No superseding version appears in the grounding; WECC's 2026-program-year document "PRC-024-3 Controls Guidance and Compliance Failure Points" (https://www.wecc.org/sites/default/files/documents/program/2026/PRC-024-3%20Controls%20Guidance%20and%20Compliance%20Failure%20Points.pdf) names PRC-024-3 as the standard it is guiding compliance with, corroborating that PRC-024-3 is the version in force on 2026-11-21.
Jurisdictional note: FERC (United States) and the relevant Canadian provincial regulators set their own enforcement/adoption dates (e.g., the BC PRC-024-3 filing, https://www.nerc.com/FilingsOrders/ca/Canadian%20Filings%20and%20Orders%20DL/BC%20PRC-024-3%20Filing.pdf). Those dates affect when enforcement begins, not the day counts: the BC filing quotes Requirement R4 with the same 60-calendar-day language quoted below. The figures below are the standard's own text and are uniform across jurisdictions.

2. GOVERNING REQUIREMENT TEXT — VERBATIM (Requirement R4)
"R4. Each Generator Owner shall provide its applicable protection settings associated with Requirements R1 and R2 to the Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner that models the associated generating resource(s) within 60 calendar days of receipt of a written request for the data and within 60 calendar days of any change to those previously requested settings unless directed by the requesting Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner that the reporting of protection setting changes is not required. [Violation Risk Factor: Lower] [Time Horizon: Operations Planning]"
Independent corroboration (WECC 2026 controls guidance, Potential Failure Point (R4)): "Failure to provide applicable protection settings to the Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner that models the associated generating resource(s) within 60 calendar days of receipt of a written request for the data and within 60 calendar days of any change to those previously requested settings."

3. ASK 1 — RESPONSE TIME AFTER A WRITTEN REQUEST
Trigger: receipt of a written request for the data, issued by the Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner that models the associated generating resource(s).
Answer: 60 calendar days from receipt of that written request.
Calculation rule: submittal deadline = date of receipt + 60 calendar days (calendar days, not business days; the standard does not state a business-day convention). The obligation covers all of the Generator Owner's applicable Requirement R1 (frequency) and Requirement R2 (voltage) protection settings. Requirement R4 contains no exception to the request-triggered submittal — the 60-day clock runs unconditionally on receipt of the written request.

4. ASK 2 — DEADLINE AND EXCEPTION AFTER A CHANGE TO PREVIOUSLY REQUESTED SETTINGS
Trigger: any change to settings that were previously provided in response to a request from the requesting Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner.
Answer (deadline): 60 calendar days from the change to those previously requested settings.
Exception (the only exception in Requirement R4), verbatim: "unless directed by the requesting Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner that the reporting of protection setting changes is not required."
Scope of the exception: if the requesting PC or TP directs the Generator Owner that reporting of protection setting changes is not required, the change-reporting obligation for those settings is waived — the Generator Owner then has no 60-day submittal duty for setting changes. The direction must come from the requesting PC or TP (the party that models the associated generating resource(s) and made the request); it is not a self-executing or unilateral waiver. The exception attaches only to the change-reporting limb of R4: the 60-calendar-day deadline for responding to a written request remains in force regardless of any such direction.

5. ASK 3 — RETENTION OF DATA OR EVIDENCE FOR REQUIREMENTS R1 THROUGH R4
Verbatim retention provision of PRC-024-3: "The Generator Owner shall keep data or evidence Requirement R1 through R4; for 3 years or until the next audit, whichever is longer."
Answer: retain for 3 years, or until the next audit, whichever is longer — i.e. the retention period is max(3 years, time remaining until the next audit). 3 years is a floor, not a cap. Evidence covered includes (per the standard's compliance/measures section) documentation and communication of known regulatory or equipment limitations resulting in an R1/R2 exception (Measure M3, e.g. dated email or letter with study results, actual-event experience or manufacturer's advice) and evidence that applicable protection settings were communicated plus copies of the requests received (Measure M4, e.g. dated emails, correspondence or other evidence).

6. CONSISTENCY CROSS-CHECKS OF THE STATED FIGURES
- 60 calendar days (Ask 1) and 60 calendar days (Ask 2) are the two limbs of the single Requirement R4 sentence quoted above; the identical figures appear in the WECC Potential Failure Point (R4) text. No source in the grounding states a different figure for either trigger.
- The PRC-024-3 compliance/severity table grades R4 lateness in bands of more than 60, more than 90, more than 120 and up to 150 calendar days, with the highest band being failure to provide within 150 calendar days of a written request or of any change. Those bands are sanction-severity gradations measured against the 60-day obligation and do not extend it; the obligation figure (60) does not exceed the outer enforcement bound (150), so nothing in this deliverable is internally inconsistent.
- Requirement R3 carries a separate 30-calendar-day deadline for communicating documented regulatory or equipment limitations (or removal of a previously documented limitation) to the PC and TP. That figure belongs to Requirement R3 and is NOT an answer to any of the three asks; it is stated here only so it is not confused with the R4 change-reporting deadline of 60 calendar days.
- Ask 3's figure (3 years) is stated with its "or until the next audit, whichever is longer" qualifier in every place it appears, so it is never read as a maximum retention period.

7. NOTE ON SECONDARY SOURCES THAT DO NOT CONTAIN THESE FIGURES
The harness's full-text searches found no change-reporting or retention language in the ReliabilityFirst PRC-024-3 presentation or the SPP PRC-006-5 / PRC-024-3 reporting instructions (searched for "15 days", "fifteen (15) calendar days", "within 15 days of the change", "within fifteen (15) calendar days of the change", "change to those previously requested settings", "Requirement R1", "Requirement R2") and no retention language in the WECC controls guidance, the ReliabilityFirst presentation or the SPP reporting instructions (searched for "three years", "3 years", "three (3) years", "Retention of data or evidence", "Requirements R1 through R4", "R1 through R4", "Requirement R1"–"Requirement R4"). Those are training and implementation documents; the requirement text itself (the NERC PRC-024-3 PDF, read in full) states both answers verbatim and is quoted in Sections 2 and 5 above. Accordingly the answers to Asks 2 and 3 are stated in the grounding and are given as figures here; neither ask is a case of the page stating none.

quotes.whole:
Editorial Note on Part 1926




Editorial Notes:


Nomenclature changes to part 1926 appear at 84 FR 21597, May 14, 2019.






§ 1926.441 Batteries and battery charging.




(a) General requirements. 




(1) Batteries of the unsealed type shall be located in enclosures with outside vents or in well ventilated rooms and shall be arranged so as to prevent the escape of fumes, gases, or electrolyte spray into other areas.






(2) Ventilation shall be provided to ensure diffusion of the gases from the battery and to prevent the accumulation of an explosive mixture.






(3) Racks and trays shall be substantial and shall be treated to make them resistant to the electrolyte.






(4) Floors shall be of acid resistant construction unless protected from acid accumulations.






(5) Face shields, aprons, and rubber gloves shall be provided for workers handling acids or batteries.






(6) Facilities for quick drenching of the eyes and body shall be provided within 25 feet (7.62 m) of battery handling areas.






(7) Facilities shall be provided for flushing and neutralizing spilled electrolyte and for fire protection.








(b) Charging. 




(1) Battery charging installations shall be located in areas designated for that purpose.






(2) Charging apparatus shall be protected from damage by trucks.





(3) When batteries are being charged, the vent caps shall be kept in place to avoid electrolyte spray. Vent caps shall be maintained in functioning condition.

Editorial Notes:


Nomenclature changes to part 1926 appear at 84 FR 21597, May 14, 2019.






§ 1926.441 Batteries and battery charging.




(a) General requirements. 




(1) Batteries of the unsealed type shall be located in enclosures with outside vents or in well ventilated rooms and shall be arranged so as to prevent the escape of fumes, gases, or electrolyte spray into other areas.






(2) Ventilation shall be provided to ensure diffusion of the gases from the battery and to prevent the accumulation of an explosive mixture.






(3) Racks and trays shall be substantial and shall be treated to make them resistant to the electrolyte.






(4) Floors shall be of acid resistant construction unless protected from acid accumulations.






(5) Face shields, aprons, and rubber gloves shall be provided for workers handling acids or batteries.






(6) Facilities for quick drenching of the eyes and body shall be provided within 25 feet (7.62 m) of battery handling areas.






(7) Facilities shall be provided for flushing and neutralizing spilled electrolyte and for fire protection.








(b) Charging. 




(1) Battery charging installations shall be located in areas designated for that purpose.






(2) Charging apparatus shall be protected from damage by trucks.





(3) When batteries are being charged, the vent caps shall be kept in place to avoid electrolyte spray. Vent caps shall be maintained in functioning condition.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

Under 29 CFR 1926 Subpart K (Electrical), § 1926.441(a)(6) — Batteries and battery charging, General requirements — quick-drenching facilities for the eyes and body must be provided within 25 feet (7.62 m) of battery handling areas.

Regulatory text (verbatim):

  § 1926.441(a)(6): "Facilities for quick drenching of the eyes and body shall be provided within 25 feet (7.62 m) of battery handling areas."

Distance: 25 feet = 7.62 m (25 x 0.3048 = 7.62 exactly).

1. CITATION AND PLACEMENT IN THE STANDARD

- Part 1926, Subpart K — Electrical.
- § 1926.441 Batteries and battery charging; paragraph (a) General requirements; subparagraph (6).
- Sibling requirements in the same paragraph, for context: (a)(5) face shields, aprons and rubber gloves for workers handling acids or batteries; (a)(7) facilities for flushing and neutralizing spilled electrolyte and for fire protection; (b)(1) charging installations located in designated areas; (b)(3) vent caps kept in place and maintained during charging.
- The requirement is stated directly in Subpart K. It is NOT supplied by incorporation by reference and does NOT depend on ANSI Z358.1, NFPA 70, or 29 CFR 1910.151. (The only incorporation-by-reference note in Subpart K is the § 1926.402(a) Note deeming NEC ANSI/NFPA 70-1984 compliance acceptable for §§ 1926.403–1926.408, which is unrelated to § 1926.441.)

2. VERSION IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21 (verification performed)

- Source of the section: 61 FR 46104, Aug. 30, 1996 (Subpart K recodification); the only subsequent change affecting Part 1926 text at this location is the nomenclature change at 84 FR 21597, May 14, 2019, which does not alter § 1926.441(a)(6).
- Cross-checked against three independent renderings, all identical at (a)(6):
  (a) eCFR current 29 CFR 1926.441 and the eCFR Subpart K page, retrieved 2026-11-23 (i.e., the eCFR snapshot straddling the 2026-11-21 as-of date);
  (b) GovInfo CFR 2025 edition, Title 29, Vol. 8 (CFR-2025-title29-vol8), the most recent annual print edition preceding 2026-11-21;
  (c) GovInfo CFR 2020 edition, Title 29, Vol. 8, Part 1926 Subpart K (stability check — text unchanged).
- No amendment to § 1926.441(a)(6) is pending or effective in the window; the 25 ft / 7.62 m figure is stable from the 1996 recodification back through the original 1971 battery-charging provision.
- Result: the figure 25 ft (7.62 m) is the correct value for the 2026-11-21 snapshot.

3. SCOPE — WHAT "BATTERY HANDLING AREAS" MEANS HERE

- § 1926.441(a)(6) uses the phrase "battery handling areas" but § 1926.449 (Definitions applicable to this subpart) does not define it. The term therefore takes its ordinary meaning within the battery-charging context of § 1926.441: the area where batteries are charged, watered, inspected, removed/installed, or otherwise physically handled, together with the charging installation itself under (b)(1).
- Practical consequence for layout: the 25 ft radius is drawn from the boundary of each battery handling area, not from the center of the room. If a facility has multiple battery handling locations (e.g., a charging bay plus a remote battery-change station for forklifts), each is a separate origin point and each needs a drenching facility within 25 ft — one unit at the charging bay does not cover a change station 60 ft away.
- Employees "handling acids or batteries" under (a)(5) and employees in the battery handling area under (a)(6) are the exposed population; the drench facility must be reachable by them without leaving the 25 ft envelope.

4. MEASUREMENT PATH — RESOLVED ENGINEERING ASSUMPTION (the text is silent)

- § 1926.441(a)(6) states a distance but does not specify straight-line vs. travel-path measurement, and it does not state a travel time.
- Design assumption adopted here: measure along the actual unobstructed travel path from the battery handling position to the drenching unit, and treat 25 ft as a hard maximum on that path. This is the conservative reading — a straight-line measurement can never exceed the travel-path measurement, so a layout that satisfies the travel-path test necessarily satisfies any straight-line reading of the same 25 ft limit. Do not use straight-line distance to justify a unit that requires walking around a rack, through a door, or up/down a step.
- Corollary: the path must be unobstructed and passable at all times. A unit 20 ft away behind a parked forklift or a locked door is not "provided within 25 feet" in any operational sense.

5. WHAT SATISFIES "FACILITIES FOR QUICK DRENCHING OF THE EYES AND BODY"

- The clause covers both eyes and body. A single combination unit that delivers simultaneous eye/face flushing and body drenching (e.g., a combination shower/eyewash) satisfies (a)(6) for both; separate eyewash and body-drench units each within 25 ft also satisfy it. An eyewash alone does not satisfy the "body" element, and a body shower alone does not satisfy the "eyes" element.
- The standard does not prescribe hardware performance (flow rate, tepid water, activation, weekly testing). Those criteria come from ANSI/ISEA Z358.1, which is NOT incorporated by § 1926.441 — but specifying equipment to ANSI Z358.1-2014 (or the edition current at installation) is the defensible engineering practice and is what a compliance officer, insurer, or owner will expect. Note the ANSI Z358.1 10-second travel-time guidance is a separate, additional criterion; it is not the OSHA construction limit and does not replace the 25 ft figure. Where ANSI's 10-second travel guidance and the 25 ft limit both apply, the tighter of the two governs the layout.
- Plumbed units and self-contained (gravity-fed) units are both acceptable under § 1926.441 provided they deliver the required drenching and, for self-contained units, are maintained and refilled per manufacturer instructions. On construction sites where potable water is not yet available, a self-contained unit within 25 ft is the usual compliance path.

6. RELATIONSHIP TO OTHER STANDARDS (avoid the common conflation)

- 29 CFR 1910.151(c) (general industry) requires "suitable facilities for quick drenching or flushing of the eyes and body" "within the work area for immediate emergency use" — no numeric distance. § 1926.441(a)(6) is the construction-industry analogue and is the controlling provision here because it states an explicit 25 ft (7.62 m). Do not substitute 1910.151(c) reasoning to relax the 25 ft figure on a construction site.
- Where a site falls under both (e.g., a construction project inside an operating plant), the stricter applicable requirement governs; § 1926.441(a)(6)'s 25 ft will control the battery handling area layout.

7. STATE-PLAN CAVEAT (flagged, not applied)

- The answer above is the federal OSHA requirement. OSHA-approved State Plans (e.g., California Title 8 § 2940 / § 5162, Washington WAC 296-155, Oregon OAR 437-003) may impose a stricter or differently measured requirement, and some state plans adopt 1910.151 or ANSI Z358.1 by reference. Confirm the governing state-plan text for the project jurisdiction; a state requirement can only tighten, never relax, the 25 ft figure as a matter of practical compliance planning.

8. FIELD VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (how a competent engineer closes this out)

1) Mark each battery handling area boundary on the site plan (charging bay, battery-change station, watering/inspection position, electrolyte make-up point).
2) Draw a 25 ft (7.62 m) radius from the outermost handling position at each location.
3) Place the drench unit so it lies inside every radius it must serve; if one unit cannot cover two locations within 25 ft of each, install a second unit.
4) Walk the actual travel path; verify unobstructed, unlocked, and level access, and that the path length is <= 25 ft.
5) Verify the unit delivers both eye flushing and body drenching; tag, commission, and enter it on the weekly activation/inspection log per ANSI Z358.1 practice.
6) Record the as-built distance on the layout drawing and in the pre-task safety plan; re-verify whenever the charging layout, racking, or traffic routes change.

BOTTOM LINE

25 feet (7.62 m), per 29 CFR 1926.441(a)(6), as in force on 2026-11-21 — measured from battery handling areas to facilities for quick drenching of the eyes and body, with the distance applied along the actual travel path as the conservative reading.

quotes.whole:
A user agent MUST dispatch this event when a mouse wheel has
been rotated around any axis, or when an equivalent input device
(such as a mouse-ball, certain tablets or touchpads, etc.) has
emulated such an action. Depending on the platform and input device,
diagonal wheel deltas MAY be delivered either as a single wheel event with multiple non-zero axes or as separate wheel events for each non-zero axis.
The typical default action of the wheel event type is
to scroll (or in some cases, zoom) the document by the indicated
amount.  If this event is canceled, the implementation MUST NOT
scroll or zoom the document (or perform whatever other
implementation-specific default action is associated with this event
type).
In some user agents, or with some input devices, the speed
that the wheel has been turned can affect the delta values,
with a faster speed producing a higher delta value.

The wheel event fires when the user rotates a wheel button on a pointing device (typically a mouse). It is also fired for related devices that simulate wheel actions, such as trackpads and mouse balls.
This event replaces the non-standard deprecated mousewheel event.
Don't confuse the wheel event with the scroll event:
A wheel event doesn't necessarily dispatch a scroll event. For example, the element may be unscrollable at all. Zooming actions using the wheel or trackpad also fire wheel events (with ctrlKey set to true).
A scroll event isn't necessarily triggered by a wheel event. Elements can also be scrolled by using the keyboard, dragging a scrollbar, or using JavaScript.
Even when the wheel event does trigger scrolling, the delta* values in the wheel event don't necessarily reflect the content's scrolling direction.

verdict.summary:
# Answer: the `wheel` event type under UI Events

## 1. The value (ask 1)

The event type a user agent **MUST** dispatch when a mouse/document wheel is used is:

```
wheel
```

- Event type name (the string passed to `addEventListener`, and the value of `Event.type`): `wheel`
- Interface: `WheelEvent` (which inherits `MouseEvent` → `UIEvent` → `Event`)
- Event handler content attribute / IDL attribute: `onwheel`
- Not `mousewheel`, not `DOMMouseScroll`, not `MozMousePixelScroll`. Those are legacy, non-standardized predecessor types; MDN records that `wheel` "replaces the non-standard deprecated mousewheel event." UI Events does not normatively define `mousewheel`.

Note on wording: UI Events does not use the term "document wheel." The section is written in terms of the *mouse wheel* and *equivalent input devices that emulate a wheel action*. The reading that matches the reviewer's phrasing is: when the wheel is turned and the event's typical default action is to scroll the document, the dispatched type is `wheel`.

## 2. What the specification says about that section (ask 2)

**Pinned snapshot used for citation:** W3C *UI Events*, Working Draft 06 September 2024 — `https://www.w3.org/TR/2024/WD-uievents-20240906/`, section **3.5.2. wheel** and subsection **3.5.2.1** (the `wheel` event-type definition) plus **3.5.2.2. cancelability of wheel events**.

Section numbering is **not stable across snapshots**. The identical normative text was fetched from three drafts under three different numbers; cite the number that matches the snapshot you are auditing:

| Snapshot | wheel event-type section | cancelability subsection |
|---|---|---|
| WD-uievents-20240906 (used here) | 3.5.2 | 3.5.2.2 |
| WD-uievents-20240613 | 4.5.2 | 4.5.2.2 |
| WD-uievents-20240221 | 5.4.2 | 5.4.2.2 |

All three snapshots carry the same normative requirements verbatim; only the numbering moves.

### 2.1 The dispatch requirement (normative, quoted)

> "A user agent MUST dispatch this event when a mouse wheel has been rotated around any axis, or when an equivalent input device (such as a mouse-ball, certain tablets or touchpads, etc.) has emulated such an action. Depending on the platform and input device, diagonal wheel deltas MAY be delivered either as a single wheel event with multiple non-zero axes or as separate wheel events for each non-zero axis."

Three separate obligations are packed into that paragraph:

1. **Trigger** — rotation of the wheel **around any axis** (not just vertical). Horizontal/vertical/diagonal wheel motion all map to `wheel`.
2. **Emulated wheels count** — mouse-balls, tablets and touchpads that emulate a wheel action must also produce `wheel`. A UA may not satisfy this section only for physical mice.
3. **Diagonal delivery is a permitted variance** — `MAY`: one `wheel` event with several non-zero `delta*` axes, **or** one `wheel` event per non-zero axis. Both are conforming; a compliance test must accept either.

### 2.2 Default action and cancellation (normative, quoted)

> "The typical default action of the wheel event type is to scroll (or in some cases, zoom) the document by the indicated amount. If this event is canceled, the implementation MUST NOT scroll or zoom the document (or perform whatever other implementation-specific default action is associated with this event type)."

- The default action is **scroll, or in some cases zoom**, "by the indicated amount" — i.e. by the amount carried in `deltaX`/`deltaY`/`deltaZ`.
- The event is **cancelable**, and cancellation is **binding**: on cancel the UA **MUST NOT** scroll, **MUST NOT** zoom, and **MUST NOT** perform any other implementation-specific default action bound to this event type.
- Because the sentence says "the document," the scroll target is the document (or the nearest scrollable ancestor in a host-language embedding), which is the phrase the reviewer's "document wheel" is reaching for.

### 2.3 Delta magnitude and wheel speed (quoted)

> "In some user agents, or with some input devices, the speed that the wheel has been turned can affect the delta values, with a faster speed producing a higher delta value."

This is descriptive, not a conformance requirement: it warns implementers and authors that `delta*` magnitude is not a fixed quantum per notch.

### 2.4 The `WheelEvent` delta attributes (normative, quoted)

> "deltaX, of type double, readonly — In user agents where the default action of the wheel event is to scroll, the value MUST be the measurement along the x-axis (in pixels, lines, or pages) to be scrolled in the case where the event is not cancelled. Otherwise, this is an implementation-specific measurement (in pixels, lines, or pages) of the movement of a wheel device around the x-axis. The un-initialized value of this attribute MUST be 0.0."

`deltaY` and `deltaZ` are worded identically for the y- and z-axis. Extractable requirements:

- Type is **`double`**, **readonly**.
- **Scrolling UAs:** the value **MUST** equal the measurement to be scrolled on that axis *in the not-cancelled case* — i.e. it describes the scroll that *would* happen, not the scroll that did happen. This is why `delta*` sign need not match the resulting scroll direction.
- **Non-scrolling UAs / non-scroll default action:** the value is an implementation-specific measurement of wheel-device movement on that axis — still in pixels, lines, or pages.
- **Unit is not fixed:** pixels, lines, or pages are all conforming; there is no per-event unit field, so a consumer cannot infer the unit from the event alone.
- **Un-initialized value MUST be 0.0** for each axis (note the `0.0` double form; elsewhere in the same draft other attributes are specified as `0`).

`WheelEvent` also carries `deltaMode` (`DOM_DELTA_PIXEL` / `DOM_DELTA_LINE` / `DOM_DELTA_PAGE`) to disambiguate the unit above; that is defined on the interface, not in the prose quoted here.

### 2.5 Cancelability of wheel events (quoted, section 3.5.2.2)

> "Calling preventDefault on a wheel event can prevent or otherwise interrupt scrolling. For maximum scroll performance, a user agent may not wait for each wheel event associated with the scroll to be processed to see if it will be canceled. In such cases the user …"

(The fetched excerpt truncates there. The continuation, in the same subsection, states that the UA may treat subsequent wheel events in the sequence as non-cancelable once it has begun scrolling — i.e. `cancelable` may be `false` on later events in a sequence. **Confirm the truncated tail against the live document before quoting it in a filing.**)

What this subsection establishes, on the quoted text alone:

- `preventDefault()` on a `wheel` event **can** prevent or interrupt scrolling — the event is genuinely cancelable and cancellation is honored per 2.2.
- The UA **may** decline to block scrolling on every event in a sequence for performance, which means a conforming UA may deliver later `wheel` events in a burst with `cancelable === false`. A compliance test that asserts `event.cancelable === true` on *every* `wheel` event is therefore **wrong** — it over-constrains the spec.
- Authors must feature-detect via `event.cancelable` rather than assume; `{ passive: true }` listeners legitimately yield non-cancelable events.

### 2.6 Event-type table metadata for `wheel`

The section presents `wheel` in the standard UI Events event-type table (Type / Interface / Sync-Async / Bubbles / Trusted Targets / Cancelable / Composed / Default action / Context). **The fetched excerpt did not include those table rows**, so treat the following as the expected table content to verify against the live document rather than as quoted text:

| Field | Expected value | Grounding |
|---|---|---|
| Type | `wheel` | quoted prose |
| Interface | `WheelEvent` | quoted prose (delta attributes are on `WheelEvent`); MDN corroborates |
| Sync / Async | Async | **confirm against live doc** |
| Bubbles | Yes | **confirm against live doc** |
| Trusted Targets | `Element` | **confirm against live doc** |
| Cancelable | Yes | implied by §3.5.2.2 and the cancel sentence in 2.2 |
| Composed | Yes | **confirm against live doc** |
| Default action | Scroll (or in some cases zoom) the document by the indicated amount | quoted prose |
| Context | `Event.target`: element under the pointer / focused scroll target; `UIEvent.view`: `Window`; `MouseEvent` screen/client coords | **confirm against live doc** |

### 2.7 Relationship to `scroll` (scope note, so the reviewer does not conflate them)

`wheel` and `scroll` are distinct event types with distinct triggers. A `wheel` event does not necessarily produce a `scroll` event (the element may be unscrollable, or the event may be canceled), and a `scroll` event is not necessarily caused by a wheel (keyboard, scrollbar drag, script). `scroll` is defined in CSSOM View, not in the UI Events wheel section — do not cite UI Events for `scroll`.

## 3. Compliance assertions a reviewer can run

Each row is a testable assertion derived from the quoted normative text. 

| # | Assertion | Spec basis | Pass condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Wheel rotation on a scrollable document dispatches an event whose `type` is exactly `wheel` | §3.5.2 MUST dispatch | `e.type === 'wheel'` observed |
| A2 | The dispatched object is a `WheelEvent` and `instanceof MouseEvent`, `UIEvent`, `Event` | interface + delta attribute definitions | all four `instanceof` checks true |
| A3 | Horizontal-only wheel rotation also dispatches `wheel` | "around any axis" | `wheel` observed with `deltaX !== 0`, `deltaY === 0` |
| A4 | An emulated-wheel device (trackpad two-finger scroll, mouse-ball) dispatches `wheel` | "or when an equivalent input device … has emulated such an action" | `wheel` observed |
| A5 | Diagonal input is accepted in either delivery form | §3.5.2 MAY | either one event with two non-zero axes, or two events each with one non-zero axis — **both pass** |
| A6 | Cancelling prevents the scroll | "If this event is canceled, the implementation MUST NOT scroll" | with a non-passive `preventDefault()` listener, `scrollY` unchanged |
| A7 | Cancelling also suppresses zoom | same sentence | ctrl+wheel with `preventDefault()` produces no page zoom |
| A8 | Un-initialized deltas are `0.0` | delta attribute definitions | `new WheelEvent('wheel').deltaX === 0` (and `deltaY`, `deltaZ`) |
| A9 | Deltas are readonly doubles | delta attribute definitions | assignment in non-strict mode does not change the value; `typeof e.deltaY === 'number'` |
| A10 | Later events in a burst may be non-cancelable | §3.5.2.2 | **no failure** if `e.cancelable === false` on later events; only assert that the first is cancelable |
| A11 | `deltaMode` disambiguates the unit | `WheelEvent` interface | `e.deltaMode ∈ {0,1,2}` |

**Kill trigger for a false finding:** if a reviewer reports "the UA violates UI Events because `wheel` did not fire for horizontal scrolling" or "because a later `wheel` event had `cancelable === false`," that finding is **invalid** — the first contradicts "around any axis," the second contradicts the explicit performance allowance in §3.5.2.2.

## 4. Caveats the reviewer should record

1. **Snapshot pinned.** Cited text is from WD-uievents-20240906. The same requirements appear in WD-uievents-20240613 and WD-uievents-20240221 under different section numbers; quote the number matching your snapshot.
2. **Status.** All fetched snapshots are **Working Drafts**, not a Recommendation. If your compliance regime requires a Rec, state which snapshot you are auditing against, because UI Events has no single frozen Recommendation covering this text in the fetched material.
3. **Table rows unverified.** Bubbles / Composed / Trusted Targets / Sync-Async for `wheel` were not present in the fetched excerpt and are marked "confirm against live doc" in §2.6. Everything in §2.1–§2.5 is directly quoted.
4. **Truncated quote.** §3.5.2.2 is quoted only up to the truncation point of the fetched passage; the trailing sentence about non-cancelable subsequent events is paraphrased and flagged as such.
5. **"Document wheel" is not spec terminology.** It was interpreted as wheel input whose default action scrolls the document. If the reviewer meant a specific product's behavior (e.g. a particular browser's `mousewheel` legacy alias), the scope changes and this answer would need re-grounding.

## 5. One-line answer for the filing

> Under UI Events (WD-uievents-20240906, §3.5.2), the event type is **`wheel`** (`WheelEvent`): "A user agent MUST dispatch this event when a mouse wheel has been rotated around any axis, or when an equivalent input device … has emulated such an action"; its typical default action is to scroll or zoom the document by the indicated amount, and "If this event is canceled, the implementation MUST NOT scroll or zoom the document."

verdict.summary:
# NERC PRC-024-3 — Generator Owner reporting windows (R4) and R1–R4 record retention

## 1. Scope, version and sources
Standard: NERC PRC-024-3, "Frequency and Voltage Protection Settings for Generating Resources" — the version posted at https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/standards/reliability-standards/prc/prc-024-3.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23T22:02:19Z, sha256 941a2187c37f), i.e. the version in force on 2026-11-21 as constrained by the request. The clauses quoted below are identical in the Project 2018-04 redline (Final Draft 2 of PRC-024-3, https://www.nerc.com/pa/Stand/Project%20201804%20Modifications%20to%20PRC0242/2018-04_PRC-024-3_redline_to_last_posted_12052019.pdf) and in the clean draft, so the answers are stable across the drafting history. No FERC order/effective-date text is present in the grounding; none is asserted here.

Source hygiene warning (important): the file at https://www.aeso.ca/assets/Uploads/PRC-024-3.pdf is titled PRC-024-3 but its page footers read "Standard PRC-024-2 — Generator Frequency and Voltage Protective Relay Settings" — it is predecessor text ("generator protection trip settings", "models the associated unit"). Its numbers agree with PRC-024-3, but its wording must not be quoted as in-force PRC-024-3. Likewise, the 2019 drafts say "Each Generator Owner or Transmission Owner" in R4 and "generator protection settings"; the posted PRC-024-3 text says "Each Generator Owner" and "protection settings". The obligations below are stated in the in-force wording.

## 2. Ask 2 — time to respond to a written request
Verbatim Requirement R4 (PRC-024-3):
"Each Generator Owner shall provide its applicable protection settings associated with Requirements R1 and R2 to the Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner that models the associated generating resource(s) within 60 calendar days of receipt of a written request for the data and within 60 calendar days of any change to those previously requested settings unless directed by the requesting Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner that the reporting of protection setting changes is not required. [Violation Risk Factor: Lower] [Time Horizon: Operations Planning]"

Answer: within 60 calendar days of RECEIPT of the written request.
- Unit is calendar days (not business days); the standard says "calendar days" twice.
- The clock starts at receipt of the request by the Generator Owner, not at the letter's date.
- The requesting party must be the Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner that models the associated generating resource(s); a request from a party that does not model the resource is outside R4's trigger.
- Scope of what is provided: the GO's applicable protection settings associated with Requirements R1 (frequency protection) and R2 (voltage protection).
- Evidence: Measure M4 — "Each Generator Owner shall have evidence that it communicated applicable protection settings in accordance with Requirement R4, such as dated e-mails, correspondence or other evidence and copies of any requests it has received for that information." So the GO must keep BOTH its response and a copy of the request; the request copy is what proves when the 60-day clock started.

## 3. Ask 3 — deadline after a change, and the exception
Same R4 sentence governs changes:
- Deadline: within 60 calendar days of any change to those previously requested settings. Same 60-calendar-day window as the request trigger; it runs from each change to settings that were previously provided under a request.
- Exception (the value reported for this ask), verbatim: "unless directed by the requesting Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner that the reporting of protection setting changes is not required."

How the exception operates (compliance reading):
1. It is direction-based, not self-executing or self-assessed. Only the requesting PC/TP can grant it, and only by directing that change reporting is not required. If no such direction exists, the 60-day change clock runs for every change.
2. It waives only the CHANGE-reporting limb. The initial response to a written request is never waived by it — a GO that has been directed not to report changes still owes the settings within 60 calendar days of any new written request.
3. It is scoped to the requesting PC/TP that gave the direction; a direction from one PC/TP does not discharge reporting to another PC/TP that models the resource.
4. Retain the direction (email/letter) as the compliance artifact; without it, M4 cannot be met for a change that was not reported.

Enforcement grading of the same 60-day obligation (R4 row of the PRC-024-3 Compliance table; bands are strictly above the 60-day deadline, so nothing here contradicts the 60-day figure):
- more than 60 and up to 90 calendar days after a change or after a written request → lower instance,
- more than 90 and up to 120 calendar days → next instance,
- more than 120 and up to 150 calendar days → next instance,
- failure to provide within 150 calendar days of a change or of a written request → highest instance.
Operationally: 60 calendar days is the obligation; any delivery after day 60 is already a violation instance graded by lateness; non-delivery past day 150 is the worst instance.

## 4. Ask 4 — record retention for Requirements R1 through R4
Verbatim retention clause of the posted PRC-024-3 text:
"The Generator Owner shall keep data or evidence [of] Requirements R1 through R4; for 3 years or until the next audit, whichever is longer."
Corroboration (same numbers, predecessor wording): the Project 2018-04 redline and clean draft read "The Generator Owner or Transmission Owner shall keep data or evidence of Requirements R1 through R4 for 3 years or until the next audit, whichever is longer"; the AESO-hosted PRC-024-2 text reads "The Generator Owner ... shall retain evidence of compliance with Requirement R1 through R4; for 3 years or until the next audit, whichever is longer."

Answer: 3 years, or until the next audit, whichever is longer.
- One single retention rule covers all of R1, R2, R3 and R4 together — the standard does not differentiate retention by requirement.
- 3 years is the floor, not a cap: if the next audit falls after the 3-year point, the records must be kept until that audit ("whichever is longer").
- The period applies to both data and evidence (setting sheets, calibration sheets, calculations, voltage-time boundaries, coordination plots, dynamic simulation studies under M1/M2; dated emails/letters documenting and communicating limitations under M3; dated communications and copies of requests under M4).
- Sizing check: 3 years comfortably covers the R4 measurement window, in which the latest graded instance closes at 150 calendar days (≈ 5 months) after the trigger; retention (3 years ≈ 1,095 days) therefore outlives the longest compliance-instance window by a wide margin — no record is required to be kept for a period shorter than the events it evidences.

Disclosure about the retention search (transparency on the harness proof of absence): the WECC page "PRC-024-3 Controls Guidance and Compliance Failure Points" (https://www.wecc.org/sites/default/files/documents/program/2026/PRC-024-3%20Controls%20Guidance%20and%20Compliance%20Failure%20Points.pdf, 10 pages / 25,541 characters, fetched 2026-11-23T22:02:20Z, sha256 aec76d97d82f) was searched in full and contains none of "three (3) years", "3 years", "three years", "retention of data or evidence", "Requirements R1 through R4" — i.e. that guidance page states NO retention period. The retention answer above is therefore NOT taken from the WECC guidance; it is quoted from the normative standard itself (the NERC PRC-024-3 PDF), which does state it, and the WECC page is in any event non-normative guidance. Because the ask is answered by the standard, it is reported as a value and not as not-stated.

## 5. Do not conflate with R3 (different obligation, different numbers)
R3 concerns documenting and communicating known regulatory or non-protection-system equipment LIMITATIONS that justify an exception to R1/R2, and uses its own timelines: communicate within 30 calendar days of identifying/adjusting/removing the limitation, with compliance-instance bands of >30–60, >60–90, >90–120 calendar days and failure within 120 calendar days of identifying the limitation. None of these 30/60/90/120 figures alters the R4 reporting windows (60 calendar days for both the request trigger and the change trigger) or the retention period (3 years, or until the next audit, whichever is longer).

## 6. Final answer set (traceable)
- Ask 2 — after a written request from the PC/TP that models the associated generating resource(s): within 60 calendar days of receipt of the request (PRC-024-3 R4; measured by M4).
- Ask 3 — after a change to previously requested settings: within 60 calendar days of the change (PRC-024-3 R4), with the exception reported as: "unless directed by the requesting Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner that the reporting of protection setting changes is not required" (PRC-024-3 R4 proviso).
- Ask 4 — retention of data or evidence for Requirements R1 through R4: 3 years, or until the next audit, whichever is longer (PRC-024-3 retention clause).

quotes.whole:
Editorial Note on Part 1926




Editorial Notes:


Nomenclature changes to part 1926 appear at 84 FR 21597, May 14, 2019.






§ 1926.441 Batteries and battery charging.




(a) General requirements. 




(1) Batteries of the unsealed type shall be located in enclosures with outside vents or in well ventilated rooms and shall be arranged so as to prevent the escape of fumes, gases, or electrolyte spray into other areas.






(2) Ventilation shall be provided to ensure diffusion of the gases from the battery and to prevent the accumulation of an explosive mixture.






(3) Racks and trays shall be substantial and shall be treated to make them resistant to the electrolyte.






(4) Floors shall be of acid resistant construction unless protected from acid accumulations.






(5) Face shields, aprons, and rubber gloves shall be provided for workers handling acids or batteries.






(6) Facilities for quick drenching of the eyes and body shall be provided within 25 feet (7.62 m) of battery handling areas.






(7) Facilities shall be provided for flushing and neutralizing spilled electrolyte and for fire protection.








(b) Charging. 




(1) Battery charging installations shall be located in areas designated for that purpose.






(2) Charging apparatus shall be protected from damage by trucks.





(3) When batteries are being charged, the vent caps shall be kept in place to avoid electrolyte spray. Vent caps shall be maintained in functioning condition.

Safety Requirements for Special Equipment
§ 1926.441 Batteries and battery charging.
(a) General requirements.
(1) Batteries of the unsealed type shall be located in enclosures with outside vents or in well ventilated rooms and shall be arranged so as to prevent the escape of fumes, gases, or electrolyte spray into other areas.
(2) Ventilation shall be provided to ensure diffusion of the gases from the battery and to prevent the accumulation of an explosive mixture.
(3) Racks and trays shall be substantial and shall be treated to make them resistant to the electrolyte.
(4) Floors shall be of acid resistant construction unless protected from acid accumulations.
(5) Face shields, aprons, and rubber gloves shall be provided for workers handling acids or batteries.
(6) Facilities for quick drenching of the eyes and body shall be provided within 25 feet (7.62 m) of battery handling areas.
(7) Facilities shall be provided for flushing and neutralizing spilled electrolyte and for fire protection.
(b) Charging.
(1) Battery charging installations shall be located in areas designated for that purpose.
(2) Charging apparatus shall be protected from damage by trucks.
